Q1.answer: Forecasting models are normalized with statistics computed on training data, so when the level of a series shifts after deployment every input is mis-scaled, producing added error. The paper addresses whether re-normalizing each input window with its own recent statistics removes that error.
Q1.missing: Prevalence of level shifts is flagged [CITATION NEEDED].

Q2.answer: Two explanations for shift-induced error compete: stale fixed normalization statistics vs. insufficient model capacity. Prior evaluations changed normalization and model size together, so the two effects were confounded and could not be separated; the paper motivates a capacity-controlled test.
Q2.missing: The claim that prior work confounds the two is unsupported ([CITATION NEEDED: literature search not yet run]).

Q3.answer: RQ1: Does normalizing each window with its own recent statistics reduce error under level shift without harming accuracy when there is no shift? RQ2: How much of any gain depends on continuing to adapt the statistics rather than re-estimating them once after the shift?

Q4.answer: (1) A capacity-controlled comparison showing RWN reduced MAE by 11–29% under shifts up to 0.6 at no unshifted cost; (2) a boundary result: no clear benefit at the largest shift (s=0.8); (3) an ablation attributing about a third of the gain to continued adaptation.

Q5.answer: A synthetic hourly series (SynthLoad) with daily/weekly cycles plus Gaussian noise, trained for one year, then tested with an added level shift of magnitude s in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8} training std, plus an unshifted period. Three normalizations compared: baseline (training mean/std), RWN (mean/std of most recent 48 steps per window), and RWN-fixed (statistics estimated once from first 48 post-shift steps then frozen). Same MLP (64 hidden units, 168h history, 24h horizon, same budget) held fixed across all; 5 seeds; report mean±std of test MAE.
Q5.missing: Whether MAE is in raw or normalized units; how SynthLoad noise/scale set.

Q6.answer: Each of the three normalization configurations was run across the shift magnitudes and the unshifted period, with 5 seeds each, and test-period MAE (mean and std) compared. The model was held identical so differences are attributed to normalization.
Q6.missing: Number of test windows / evaluation horizon detail.

Q7.answer: Without shift: RWN 0.409±0.007 vs baseline 0.412±0.006 (indistinguishable). Under shift up to s=0.6 RWN's error stayed near its unshifted level while baseline's rose; at s=0.6 RWN reduced MAE from 0.641 to 0.452, a reduction of 11–29% across s=0.2–0.6, with seed spread ≤0.012. At s=0.8 RWN 0.712±0.021 vs baseline 0.731±0.015 (gap ~one std, no clear benefit). Ablation: RWN-fixed 0.518 at s=0.6, recovering ~2/3 of the gain; remaining ~1/3 from continued adaptation.
Q7.missing: Exact per-shift MAE values for s=0.2 and s=0.4 (only the 11–29% range given).

Q8.answer: Because the model was identical across conditions, the results suggest that stale normalization statistics, rather than model capacity, account for much of the baseline's shift-induced error in this setting. The authors explicitly frame this as an interpretation, noting capacity was held constant, not varied, so the capacity explanation was not directly tested.

Q9.answer: Limitations: (1) all data from one synthetic generator, so transfer to real load series untested; (2) window length (48) not tuned, so gains describe one untuned setting; (3) only level shifts studied — no claim about variance/seasonality shifts; and no benefit at the largest shift.

Q10.answer: So-what: in a capacity-controlled synthetic setting, post-shift error appears to stem mostly from stale normalization statistics; re-estimating them per window removes most of that error for moderate shifts without harming unshifted accuracy, but the benefit vanishes at the largest shift. Open question: whether it holds on real load data and larger models.

Q11.answer: Key terms: RWN = rolling-window normalization (per-window mean/std of most recent 48 steps); RWN-fixed = re-estimate once post-shift then freeze; baseline = training mean/std; s = shift magnitude in units of training standard deviations; MAE reported as mean±std over 5 seeds.
Q11.missing: MAE unit basis (raw vs normalized) not stated; '48 steps' vs hourly not explicitly linked to hours.

Q12.answer: The finding stops at: moderate shifts only (no benefit at s=0.8); one synthetic data generator (real-data transfer untested); one untuned window length; and level shifts only (no variance/seasonality). The interpretation that capacity is not the cause is bounded because capacity was held constant, not varied.

objective_discrepancies: The objective promises the reader will know 'what was tested' fully, but per-shift MAE for s=0.2 and s=0.4 is only given as an aggregate 11–29% range, limiting exact reconstruction.

The objective centers on real-world relevance (level shifts after deployment) yet all evidence is from a single synthetic generator; the gap between stated motivation and evidence base is acknowledged but wide for the intended robustness audience.
Unresolved [CITATION NEEDED] and [ASK AUTHOR] markers remain in the text, which conflicts with delivering a reader who comes away knowing where the finding stops on a verifiable basis.
